who: Color vision deficiency — about 1 in 12 men
takeaways: Pair every color cue with a second one: text, an icon, a pattern, a shape or position.
Links inside body text need an underline — or 3:1 contrast with surrounding text plus a non-color cue on hover and focus.
In charts, label lines and areas directly instead of relying on a color legend.
Errors and required fields need words, not just red.
failures: Form errors shown only by a red border
Red and green status dots with no label
Line charts where series differ only by hue
check: View the screen in grayscale. Is anything lost?
Run it through a color-blindness simulator.
For each color you use, ask: what else tells people this?

quiz.question: Required fields are marked only by red labels. Which fix satisfies 1.4.1?
options: Add “(required)” or an asterisk with a legend
quiz.why: Changing the color doesn’t help — the cue can’t depend on color at all. Text or a symbol does.

spec: Beside each status color, write its second cue: icon, label or pattern.
Specify links inside body text as underlined by default.
In charts, note the direct label and the marker or pattern for each series.
review: If this screen were printed in gray, what would be lost?
Which states differ only by hue?
Does the chart still read without its legend colors?
tradeoff: Extra icons and labels add noise. The answer is a quieter second cue, such as weight, position or a small glyph. It is not removing the cue.
system: Build the second cue into status components (badge, alert, field error) so nobody can ship color alone.
pitch: About 1 in 12 men has a color vision deficiency. A color-only status is invisible to someone in almost every team that uses your product.
